Hi all,

I have a question, it may be very easy and basic, so, sorry about that.
I know that there are three diferents model averaging:
1. Model averaging suggested by Burnham and Anderson (2002) or
2. Natural averaging mencionated by Symmonds and Moussalli (2011) or
3. Full-model averaging mencionated by Symmonds and Moussalli (2011)

So, my question would be: What kind of model averaging applies unmarked?

Thanks for your answers, I really appreciate your help.

Burnham and Anderson. 2002. Model Selection and Multimodel Inference: A Practical Information-Theoretic Approach
Symmonds and Moussalli. 2011.A brief guide to model selection, multimodel inference and model averaging in behavioural  ecology using Akaike’s information criterion

messages.body_plain:
Hi Alejandro,

in the package AICcmodavg, modavg( ) implements natural averaging of beta estimates as discussed in Burnham and Anderson (2002), modavgShrink( ) implements the shrinkage estimator on beta estimates (also discussed in Burnham and Anderson 2002, p. 152; and Luckacs et al. 2010: Model selection bias and Freedman's paradox. Annals of the Institute of Statistical Mathematics 62:117-125). You can also model-average predictions or effect sizes (differences between specific groups) with modavgPred( ) and modavgEffect( ) - both implement the shrinkage estimator.

The natural average estimator is known to be biased, especially when the variable appears in models that do not have a lot of support (see Cade, B. S. 2015. Model averaging and muddled multimodel inferences. Ecology 96:2370-2382).

Hope it helps,

Marc

I think the last two options you refer to involve averaging coefficients, which (intentionally) isn't possible in unmarked. messages.body_plain:
Dear everyone!

I am very new to unmarked and statistics, so please excuse any imprecise wording, I’ll give my best to explain what I need though. I am working on modelling detection probability and abundance of different bird species from repeated point counts (55 sites, visited twice in a single season with 4 x 5 minutes consecutively following each other for both visits). I use three detection covariables (start time of count, day of the year and number of birds present per count) and three abundance variables (relative open, forest and urban area) for each of 37 species recorded. For the abundance variables, I use the composition of habitats, relative to the area within the first 300 meters around my point in percent (which covers all observations). Therefore, 100, 0 and 0 would indicate a purely open habitat (always adding up to 100%). I scaled all these variables, both for the state and the detection process.

Everything works fine as long as I set abundance to 1 and try finding the best model for modelling the detection process first (which is coincides with what I have read in this group before asking my question). However, as soon as I start modelling the abundance, my abundance p-values go to 1.00 for each of the covariables and I do think that this is highly unlikely. This happens with all the species I tried it so far (more than 20) and I think that my problem might have to do with the form of the parameters I model abundance with? Is it possible to model abundance by these three covariables that add up to 1 respectively or is this my problem?

Example of one of the species:

Abundance:

            Estimate       SE         z  P(>|z|)

(Intercept)   0.7651    0.136  5.61e+00 2.05e-08

Open_Area     0.0221 3799.524  5.83e-06 1.00e+00

Forest_Area  -0.0567 2966.185 -1.91e-05 1.00e+00

Urban_Area    0.0242 3449.209  7.00e-06 1.00e+00

Detection:

            Estimate    SE      z  P(>|z|)

(Intercept)  -0.9477 0.163 -5.809 6.29e-09

StartTime    -0.2221 0.116 -1.907 5.65e-02

DayNr        -0.0272 0.101 -0.271 7.86e-01

ObsNr         0.6432 0.111  5.779 7.53e-09

I am sorry if this is a very fundamental question and can be simply answered with: “Christian, that’s the worst thing you can ever do and does not make any sense at all” but I both hope this is not the case and someone can help me out with finding a solution.

Thanks a lot for your time in advance, Christian

Dear Christian,

messages.body_plain:
It's a collinearity issue.  When the proportions sum to 1, it is not possible to distinguish between predictor effects: the variables are perfectly collinear, because the value of %open can be perfectly predicted given knowledge of %forest and %urban. Brian Cade discusses this a bit in his 2015 paper in Ecology (Model averaging and muddled multi-model inferences) while pointing out flaws in a previous analysis. (The paper is not entirely focused on collinearity/identifiability, but the most recent thing I could think of that had some basis in habitat modeling).

Cheers,

John

Dear Pat,

Couple of things:

(1)    First, whether you get reliable inference or not in the RN depends a lot on how well the parametric assumptions of this model are met. Or rather, how badly they are violated. The RN model is much more sensitive to the parametric assumptions than many other hierarchical models, such as binomial or multinomial mixture models or occupancy models. ---- Presumably, you can do some GOF test to get a feel for this, though we never know whether the test is sensitive at all or to specific assumption violations, for lack of studies

(2)    When abundance is very high, there may be little or now variation in p with which to estimate variation in abundance

(3)    And then there is the first law of capture-recapture: when p gets small, things become screwy.

The last one is actually the simplest and you can explore this using simulation, using exactly your sample sizes (N sites, N visits) and presumed parameter values (abundance and detection). The first one is the most difficult one.

Best regards --  Marc

Dear Augusto,

I think you must be right and about the AHMbook zip being only for Windows users. We have to see how to format that into a tar to let Linux users enjoy the package.

The sim function in chapter 1 is in the R package. For your convenience, it’s repeated down here.

Best regards  --- Marc

sim.fn <- function (quad.size = 10, cell.size = 1, intensity = 1, show.plot = TRUE)

{

    exp.M <- intensity * quad.size^2

    breaks <- seq(0, quad.size, cell.size)

    n.cell <- (quad.size/cell.size)^2

    mid.pt <http://mid.pt> <- breaks[-length(breaks)] + 0.5 * cell.size

    M <- rpois(1, exp.M)

    u1 <- runif(M, 0, quad.size)

    u2 <- runif(M, 0, quad.size)

    N <- as.matrix(table(cut(u1, breaks = breaks), cut(u2, breaks = breaks)))

    lambda <- round(mean(N), 2)

    var <- var(c(N))

    z <- N

    z[z > 1] <- 1

    psi <- mean(z)

    if (show.plot) {

        par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(5, 5, 5, 2), cex.lab = 1.5,

            cex.axis = 1.3, cex.main = 1.3)

        plot(u1, u2, xlab = "x coord", ylab = "y coord", cex = 1,

            pch = 16, asp = 1, main = paste("Point pattern: \nIntensity =",

                intensity, ", M =", M, "inds."), xlim = c(0,

                quad.size), ylim = c(0, quad.size), frame = F,

            col = "red")

        polygon(c(0, quad.size, quad.size, 0), c(0, 0, quad.size,

            quad.size), lwd = 3, col = NA, border = "black")

        plot(u1, u2, xlab = "x coord", ylab = "y coord", cex = 1,

            pch = 16, asp = 1, main = paste("Abundance pattern: \nRealized mean density =",

                lambda, "\nSpatial variance =", round(var, 2)),

            xlim = c(0, quad.size), ylim = c(0, quad.size), frame = F,

            col = "red")

        for (i in 1:length(breaks)) {

            for (j in 1:length(breaks)) {

                segments(breaks[i], breaks[j], rev(breaks)[i],

                  breaks[j])

                segments(breaks[i], breaks[j], breaks[i], rev(breaks)[j])

            }

        }

        for (i in 1:length(mid.pt <http://mid.pt>)) {

            for (j in 1:length(mid.pt <http://mid.pt>)) {

                text(mid.pt <http://mid.pt>[i], mid.pt <http://mid.pt>[j], N[i, j], cex = 10^(0.8 -

                  0.4 * log10(n.cell)), col = "blue")

            }

        }

        polygon(c(0, quad.size, quad.size, 0), c(0, 0, quad.size,

            quad.size), lwd = 3, col = NA, border = "black")

        plot(u1, u2, xlab = "x coord", ylab = "y coord", cex = 1,

            pch = 16, asp = 1, main = paste("Occurrence pattern: \nRealized occupancy =",

                round(psi, 2)), xlim = c(0, quad.size), ylim = c(0,

                quad.size), frame = F, col = "red")

        for (i in 1:length(breaks)) {

            for (j in 1:length(breaks)) {

                segments(breaks[i], breaks[j], rev(breaks)[i],

                  breaks[j])

                segments(breaks[i], breaks[j], breaks[i], rev(breaks)[j])

            }

        }

        for (i in 1:(length(breaks) - 1)) {

            for (j in 1:(length(breaks) - 1)) {

                polygon(c(breaks[i], breaks[i + 1], breaks[i +

                  1], breaks[i]), c(breaks[j], breaks[j], breaks[j +

                  1], breaks[j + 1]), col = "black", density = z[i,

                  j] * 100)

            }

        }

        polygon(c(0, quad.size, quad.size, 0), c(0, 0, quad.size,

            quad.size), lwd = 3, col = NA, border = "black")

        plot(table(N), xlab = "Abundance (N)", ylab = "Number of cells",

            col = "black", xlim = c(0, max(N)), main = "Frequency of N with mean density (blue)",

            lwd = 3, frame = F)

        abline(v = lambda, lwd = 3, col = "blue")

    }

    return(list(quad.size = quad.size, cell.size = cell.size,

        intensity = intensity, exp.N = exp.M, breaks = breaks,

        n.cell = n.cell, mid.pt <http://mid.pt> = mid.pt <http://mid.pt>, M = M, u1 = u1, u2 = u2,

        N = N, z = z, psi = psi))

}

The monitoring program uses automated recording devices deployed for multiple nights. There is a need for guidance on the workflow for analyses of the resulting acoustic data as well as on how to account for species misidentification within occupancy models and how to properly account for the inherent uncertainty in the acoustic data.

Summarize current knowledge and procedures used by NABat and their partners.

b.      Explore current Bayesian occupancy models to account for species classification errors based on acoustic data. Provide guidance on the use of such methods for practitioners, as applied to acoustic bat datasets with accompanying code and worked examples. Here is a brute force approach using the Delta method.  (I can supply the details for the estimate of the standard error later this week when I have more time.)

# Two-visit example to get approximate confidence intervals for big P

# Load library
  library(unmarked)

# Generate some data from known parameters
# Number of sites
  n <- 100
# Site status
  psi <- 0.8 # Probability of occupancy
  status <- rbinom(n,1,psi)
# Observation status
  p1 <- 0.90
  y1 <- rbinom(n,1,p1)
  p2 <- 0.56
  y2 <- rbinom(n,1,p2)
  y <- status*matrix(c(y1,y2),byrow=FALSE,nrow=n)
# Visit number
  visit =matrix(rep(c("1","2"),n),byrow=TRUE,nrow=n)

# Make unmarked data frame
  udf <- unmarkedFrameOccu(y,obsCovs=list(visit=visit))

# Run occu
  results = occu(~ visit ~ 1, udf)

# Get estimates
  # logits of detection parameters from occu
  intercept = results@estimates@estimates$det@estimates[1]
  visit2 = results@estimates@estimates$det@estimates[2]
  # Covariance matrix of detection logits
  covmat = results@estimates@estimates$det@covMat
  # Detection probabilities for visits 1 and 2
  p1.mle = 1 - 1/(1+exp(intercept))
  p2.mle = 1 - 1/(1+exp(intercept+visit2))
  # Probability of at least one detection at an occupied site
  bigP.mle = 1 - (1-p1.mle)*(1-p2.mle)
  # Approximate standard error of bigP using the Delta method
    bigP.se = ((exp(2*intercept)*(covmat[1,1]*(1 + exp(visit2) +
      2*exp(intercept + visit2))^2 + exp(visit2)*(1 + exp(intercept))*
      (covmat[2,2]*exp(visit2)*(1 + exp(intercept)) + 2*covmat[1,2]*(1 + exp(visit2) +
      2*exp(intercept + visit2)))))/ ((1 + exp(intercept))^4*
      (1 + exp(intercept + visit2))^4))^0.5
  # Approximate confidence intervals for bigP
  lower95 = max(0,bigP.mle - 1.96*bigP.se)
  upper95 = min(1,bigP.mle + 1.96*bigP.se)

# Summarize results
  cat("True bigP = 1 - (1-p1)*(1-p2) = ",1 - (1-p1)*(1-p2),"\n")
  cat("Estimate of bigP = ",bigP.mle,"\n")
  cat("Approximate 95% confidence interval for bigP = (",lower95,",",upper95,")\n")

Well, it was much simpler than I made it out to be.  If one has no observation covariates other than the visit number (as a string), then running occu with

     results = occu(~ -1 + visit ~ 1, udf)

such that each visit gets an explicit logit to itself, life becomes much simpler.  Below is the updated example still with just 2 visits in the simulated data but the formulas for the standard error (and confidence intervals) will work with any number of visits.  (Someone must have done this before but I'm sorry not to know who that is.)

# Two-visit example to get approximate confidence intervals for big P

# Load library
  library(unmarked)

# Generate some data from known parameters
# Number of sites
  n <- 100
# Site status
  psi <- 0.8 # Probability of occupancy
  status <- rbinom(n,1,psi)

  p2 <- 0.56

# Make unmarked data frame
  udf <- unmarkedFrameOccu(y,obsCovs=list(visit=visit))

# Run occu

  results = occu(~ -1 + visit ~ 1, udf)

# Covariance matrix for logits
  covmat = results@estimates@estimates$det@covMat

# Detection probabilities for each visit
  p.mle <- matrix(1 - 1/(1+exp(results@estimates@estimates$det@estimates)),nrow=1)

# Approximate standard error for big P

Hi Alejandro,

the statement regarding model-averaging beta estimates using the shrinkage estimator is a limit of the method. You should be careful when model-averaging beta estimates using any estimator. A beta estimate of a variable appearing in a model that also involves the same variable in an interaction (i.e., polynomial effects or other interactions) is not directly comparable to a beta estimate appearing in a model without such effects. This is one reason why some avoid model-averaging beta estimates and focus on real estimates instead, such as effect sizes (see ?modavgEffect).

Hope it helps,

Marc

hi Myles,

 With fairly complex models there is a chance of numerical crashes in the optimization and unfortunately our fitting functions are not robust to this, so this can cause problems in the context of simulation studies such as when doing the parametric bootstrapping.  The solution to this is to do the parametric bootstrapping "the long way" -- i.e., do all the simulation, fitting, and summarizing outside of the parboot function.  Another option is to figure out how to rewrite the parboot using the trycatch() function which I've heard people mention before but I'm afraid I don't know how to do that.

 With regard to your second question: if you're simulating data and then fitting the data-generating model then it should pass the  bootstrap goodness-of-fit.... unfortunately I can't take the time right now to search through your simulation code but I suggest starting with the simplest possible model to verify that and then hunt down your probable bug.

 I wonder if anyone on the unmarked list has tried such a simulation study before and, if so, what was the result?

 In general, there is a need for simulation studies on the power of these tests under various alternatives. It would be a good paper to write if anyone is interested.

regards
andy

Second, to expand on what Andy stated about numerical crashes:  Even with all of the resources thrown at PROC MIXED and PROC GLIMMIX in SAS along with mixed models in R using lme4, numerical issues dominate the time I spend dealing with such analyses. Jim

Dear all,

just let me throw some code example out for the use of the R function try() to prevent unmarked from crashing when a numerical error occurs. From some Nmix modeling that I did for a very large number of species and scenarios. Hope this is understandable and you can adapt it to your case.

Best regards  --- Marc

      # Fit model with Poisson mixture and do parametric bootstrap GOF
      fmP <- try(pcount(~date+I(date^2) ~forest+elev+I(elev^2), umf, control=list(trace=TRUE,
          REPORT=5, maxit = 300)))
      if (class(fmP) == "try-error") {v<-1} else {
      tmpP <- summary(fmP)
      (pbP <- parboot(fmP, fitstats, nsim=n.boot, report=1))
      stats <- extract.parboot(pbP)
      results[row.number,6:12] <- coef(fmP)
      results[row.number,13:16] <- tmpP$state[,2]
      results[row.number,17:19] <- tmpP$det[,2]
      results[row.number,20] <- fmP@negLogLike
      results[row.number,21] <- fmP@AIC
      results[row.number,22:24] <- stats[,7]
      results[row.number,25:27] <- stats[,6]
      }

Hello Group,

This may be a very basic question, but for the life of me I cannot find reference to it in any forum post or paper. If I want to make predictions for future years in a dynamic occupancy model, how would I go about that without having to do all the math by hand? I understand I'll need to make some assumptions, like my covariates won't change (I am not using climate and thus cannot rely on GCMs, and I have no future land use models, etc.), and that future species-environment relationships won't change, and probably some more I can't think of right now.

I have data for 2010-2015, and the model returns estimates for psi at 2010-2015, and for col and ext at 2010-2014. This makes sense because the model needs occupancy estimates at 2015 to calculate col and ext at 2014 (right?). So how can calculate psi for 2016 if I don't have col and ext estimates for 2015? How would I go about calculating those?

I'm using the maximum likelihood-based `colext()` function in unmarked, and was wondering if there is a nice way to make future predictions with the available functions. Or is this only viable/tenable using Bayesian methods?

My apologies for the mass of questions. Please be merciful if I'm asking something dumb. Thank you all.

- Jamie

Dear Jamie,

there are a couple of ways how you could make such forecasts, and they differ in their degree of sophistication.
(1) You could assume that the year effects that you have estimated are characteristic of the annual variation in the system and write R code that takes occupancy for every site for the last year (2015) and then randomly picks one of the interannual values of colonisation and extinction to produce an estimate of occupancy in 2016. You repeat this 1000 times or so and take the average as your point estimate and the 2.5 and 97.5 percentiles as your 95% confidence limits. This you could do directly with the output from your analysis in unmarked.
(2) A better approach would be to fit the model with colonisation and extinction both specified as yearly random effects. When you then predict to 2016, you directly get a posterior distribution of the occupancy forecast. This you would most likely have to do with BUGS.

No doubt there are other methods. The first one is what matrix population modellers sometimes did (at least up to about 15 years ago) in population viability analyses. The latter one is a more elegant solution which is trivial with bayesian MCMC.

If this important to you, then it would be worthwhile to read around how people do such forecasts in other fields of ecology, especially population modeling.

Best regards  --  Marc

Here is something specific when year is treated as a continuous covariate and not as a factor which allows one to make predictions for future years.  What I do is augment the original unmarkedMultFrame with the future covariates and make all of the associated observations NA.  Running colext ignores those missing values for estimation purposes but does construct the predictions for all because the covariates are present.  (Of course, one needs to check model fit and rationalize that future observations are likely to result from at least a similar model.)

Below is an example modified from the vignette "Dynamic occupancy models in unmarked" by Marc Kery and Richard Chandler.

> # Load library
>   library(unmarked)
>
> # Simulate some data
>   M <- 250 # Number of sites
>   J <- 3 # num secondary sample periods
>   T <- 10 # num primary sample periods
>   psi <- rep(NA, T) # Occupancy probability
>   muZ <- z <- array(dim = c(M, T)) # Expected and realized occurrence
>   y <- array(NA, dim = c(M, J, T)) # Detection histories
>   set.seed(13973)
>   psi[1] <- 0.4 # Initial occupancy probability
>   p <- rep(0.6,T)
>   # Extinction probability:  logit is linear in year
>   epsilon <- 1 - 1/(1+exp(0.1-0.3*(1:(T-1)))) # Extinction probability
>   phi <- 1 - epsilon
>   gamma <- 1 - 1/(1+exp(0.3+0.3*(1:(T-1)))) # Colonization probability
>   # Generate latent states of occurrence
>   # First year
>   z[,1] <- rbinom(M, 1, psi[1]) # Initial occupancy state
> # Later years
>   for(i in 1:M){ # Loop over sites
>      for(k in 2:T){ # Loop over years
>         muZ[k] <- z[i, k-1]*phi[k-1] + (1-z[i, k-1])*gamma[k-1]
>         z[i,k] <- rbinom(1, 1, muZ[k])
>      }
>   }
> # Generate detection/non-detection data
>   for(i in 1:M){
>      for(k in 1:T){
>         prob <- z[i,k] * p[k]
>         for(j in 1:J){
>            y[i,j,k] <- rbinom(1, 1, prob)
>         }
>      }
>   }
>
> # Make unmarkedMultFrame for original data
>   yy <- matrix(y, M, J*T)
>   year <- matrix(c(1:10), nrow(yy), T, byrow=TRUE)
>   simUMF <- unmarkedMultFrame(y = yy, yearlySiteCovs = list(year = year),
>     numPrimary=T)
>
> # Analysis before augmenting with "future" observations
>   m  <- colext(psiformula= ~1, gammaformula = ~ year, epsilonformula = ~ year,
>     pformula = ~ 1, data = simUMF, method="BFGS")
>   summary(m)
>
> # Add columns to yy and year associated with a future year
> # Actual values go into year.future and missing values go into yy.future
> # (Predictions for multiple future years can also be added here)
>   yy.future = cbind(yy,matrix(rep(NA,M*J),nrow=M))
>   # Here I've added year T+1 but any other year could be added
>   year.future <- cbind(year,matrix(rep(T+1,M),nrow=M))
>   simUMF.future <- unmarkedMultFrame(y = yy.future,
>     yearlySiteCovs = list(year = year.future), numPrimary=T+1)
>
> # Run colext on augmented data
>   m.future <- colext(psiformula= ~1, gammaformula = ~ year,
>     epsilonformula = ~ year, pformula = ~ 1, data = simUMF.future, method="BFGS")
>   summary(m.future)
>
> # Make predictions
>   m.fu...@projected.mean
>   m.fu...@smoothed.mean

What I do is augment the original unmarkedMultFrame with the future covariates and make all of the associated observations NA.  Running colext ignores those missing values for estimation purposes but does construct the predictions for all because the covariates are present.  (Of course, one needs to check model fit and rationalize that future observations are likely to result from at least a similar model.)
>
> Below is an example modified from the vignette "Dynamic occupancy models in unmarked" by Marc Kery and Richard Chandler.
>
> > # Load library
> >   library(unmarked)
> >
> > # Simulate some data
> >   M <- 250 # Number of sites
> >   J <- 3 # num secondary sample periods
> >   T <- 10 # num primary sample periods
> >   psi <- rep(NA, T) # Occupancy probability
> >   muZ <- z <- array(dim = c(M, T)) # Expected and realized occurrence
> >   y <- array(NA, dim = c(M, J, T)) # Detection histories
> >   set.seed(13973)
> >   psi[1] <- 0.4 # Initial occupancy probability
> >   p <- rep(0.6,T)
> >   # Extinction probability:  logit is linear in year
> >   epsilon <- 1 - 1/(1+exp(0.1-0.3*(1:(T-1)))) # Extinction probability
> >   phi <- 1 - epsilon
> >   gamma <- 1 - 1/(1+exp(0.3+0.3*(1:(T-1)))) # Colonization probability
> >   # Generate latent states of occurrence
> >   # First year
> >   z[,1] <- rbinom(M, 1, psi[1]) # Initial occupancy state
> > # Later years
> >   for(i in 1:M){ # Loop over sites
> >      for(k in 2:T){ # Loop over years
> >         muZ[k] <- z[i, k-1]*phi[k-1] + (1-z[i, k-1])*gamma[k-1]
> >         z[i,k] <- rbinom(1, 1, muZ[k])
> >      }
> >   }
> > # Generate detection/non-detection data
> >   for(i in 1:M){
> >      for(k in 1:T){
> >         prob <- z[i,k] * p[k]
> >         for(j in 1:J){
> >            y[i,j,k] <- rbinom(1, 1, prob)
> >         }
> >      }
> >   }
> >
> > # Make unmarkedMultFrame for original data
> >   yy <- matrix(y, M, J*T)
> >   year <- matrix(c(1:10), nrow(yy), T, byrow=TRUE)
> >   simUMF <- unmarkedMultFrame(y = yy, yearlySiteCovs = list(year = year),
> >     numPrimary=T)
> >
> > # Analysis before augmenting with "future" observations
> >   m  <- colext(psiformula= ~1, gammaformula = ~ year, epsilonformula = ~ year,
> >     pformula = ~ 1, data = simUMF, method="BFGS")
> >   summary(m)
> >
> > # Add columns to yy and year associated with a future year
> > # Actual values go into year.future and missing values go into yy.future
> > # (Predictions for multiple future years can also be added here)
> >   yy.future = cbind(yy,matrix(rep(NA,M*J),nrow=M))
> >   # Here I've added year T+1 but any other year could be added
> >   year.future <- cbind(year,matrix(rep(T+1,M),nrow=M))
> >   simUMF.future <- unmarkedMultFrame(y = yy.future,
> >     yearlySiteCovs = list(year = year.future), numPrimary=T+1)
> >
> > # Run colext on augmented data
> >   m.future <- colext(psiformula= ~1, gammaformula = ~ year,
> >     epsilonformula = ~ year, pformula = ~ 1, data = simUMF.future, method="BFGS")
